title: Genesis 20 — Avraham at Gerar and the wife-sister episode with Avimelekh

verdicts.reasoning: Standard ASV rendering of וַיִּסַּע / וַיֵּשֶׁב / וַיָּגָר; lexical choices (journeyed / dwelt / sojourned) preserve the three distinct verbs of motion-and-settlement. Defensible without dispute.

citations: Alter, The Art of Biblical Narrative 1981, pp. 47-62 (type-scene)
verdicts.reasoning: אֲחֹתִי הִוא rendered 'She is my sister' (ASV); the *va-yiqach* taking-verb is preserved (echoing Gen 12:15 *va-tuqach*). The commentary's structural note on the type-scene's narrator-presentation (deception unattributed; rationale supplied retrospectively at vv 11-13) is mainstream (Sarna, Alter).

citations: Husser, Dreams and Dream Narratives in the Biblical World 1999
Oppenheim, The Interpretation of Dreams in the Ancient Near East 1956
verdicts.reasoning: First-occurrence claim for the *va-yavo Elohim el-X ba-chalom ha-lailah* formula verified against the canonical Hebrew sequence — no prior *chalom* dream-revelation exists in Genesis 1-19 (the Gen 15:12 *tardemah* is a deep-sleep, not a dream). Cross-corpus parallels (Gen 28:12, 31:24, 37, 40-41, 1 Kgs 3:5) and the Num 12:6 ranking are accurately documented.

הֲגוֹי גַּם־צַדִּיק תַּהֲרֹג rendered 'will you slay even a righteous nation?' — the *gam*-as-concessive is correctly read. The verbal echo of Gen 18:23-25 (Sarna, Wenham) is genuine and well-attested.

citations: Kraus, Psalms 1-59 1988 on Ps 24:4 and Ps 26:6
verdicts.reasoning: Doubled-noun בְּתָם־לְבָבִי וּבְנִקְיֹן כַּפַּי preserved literally ('integrity of my heart and cleanness of my hands'); inward / outward register-pairing documented from Ps 24:4 and Ps 73:13. Forensic-moral idiom reading is mainstream (Kraus, Sarna).

Reduction of the doubled formula to *tom levav* alone is correctly read as the narrative's pair-and-reduce structure (Avimelekh pleads both registers; Elohim acknowledges the inward one because restraint prevented the outward act). Defensible reading.

citations: Wilson, Prophecy and Society in Ancient Israel 1980
verdicts.reasoning: MANDATORY MAJOR: Gen 20:7 verified as the first *navi* occurrence in the canonical Hebrew Bible (no prior occurrence in Gen 1-19; Exod 7:1 and the Deuteronomic frame follow in canonical sequence). The paratactic function-definition (*navi hu v-yitpallel*) is textually explicit. ASV-baseline 'prophet' over Speiser's 'spokesman' is the lexically-consistent choice. Cross-corpus intercession chain (Exod 32, Num 14, 1 Sam 7/12, Jer 7/11/14, Amos 7) is documentary. Cited scholarship (Lindblom 1962, Wilson 1980, Petersen 2002, Sarna JPS 1989 pp.142-143) is mainstream and standard.
Standard rendering; וַיִּירְאוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים מְאֹד preserves the *y-r-a* root linking to v 11's *yir'at Elohim* — appropriately uncommented in the verse but available via the v 11 glossary entry.

citations: Alter, The Art of Biblical Narrative 1981
verdicts.reasoning: Echo of Gen 12:18 (*mah-zot asita li*) and forward-reach to Gen 26:10 is accurate type-scene observation (Alter; Sarna). The 'deeds that ought not to be done' rendering of *ma'asim asher lo ye'asu* preserves ASV's modal force.
מָה רָאִיתָ literally 'what did you see' (idiomatic 'what were you thinking') preserved; defensible.

Cross-corpus *yir'at Elohim* chain (Gen 22:12 Aqedah, Gen 42:18 Joseph, Exod 1:17 midwives, Exod 20:20 Sinai, Job 1:1, Prov 1:7, Eccl 12:13) verified; Becker 1965 *Gottesfurcht im AT* is the standard monograph. paragraphs.text: וַיִּסַּ֨ע מִשָּׁ֤ם אַבְרָהָם֙ אַ֣רְצָה הַנֶּ֔גֶב וַיֵּ֥שֶׁב בֵּין־קָדֵ֖שׁ וּבֵ֣ין שׁ֑וּר וַיָּ֖גָר בִּגְרָֽר׃

i18n.en: And Abraham journeyed from there toward the land of the Negev, and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur; and he sojourned in Gerar.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר אַבְרָהָ֛ם אֶל־שָׂרָ֥ה אִשְׁתּ֖וֹ אֲחֹ֣תִי הִ֑וא וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח אֲבִימֶ֙לֶךְ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ גְּרָ֔ר וַיִּקַּ֖ח אֶת־שָׂרָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, She is my sister: and Avimelekh king of Gerar sent, and took Sarah.

paragraphs.commentary: The second instance of the wife-sister type-scene (Gen 12, 20, 26; see [wife-sister-type-scene](#wife-sister-type-scene)). The sister-claim here is unattributed-to-anyone — Abraham *said of Sarah his wife, She is my sister* — without the earlier *imri-na achoti at* coaching-speech form of Gen 12:13. The chapter's narrator presents the deception at a remove; the rationale will be retrospectively supplied by Abraham at vv 11-13. The verb *va-yiqach* (*and he took*) is the same taking-verb used at Gen 12:15 (*va-tuqach ha-ishah*); the type-scene vocabulary is being deliberately reused.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֧א אֱלֹהִ֛ים אֶל־אֲבִימֶ֖לֶךְ בַּחֲל֣וֹם הַלָּ֑יְלָה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ הִנְּךָ֥ מֵת֙ עַל־הָאִשָּׁ֣ה אֲשֶׁר־לָקַ֔חְתָּ וְהִ֖וא בְּעֻ֥לַת בָּֽעַל׃

i18n.en: But the Elohim came to Avimelekh in a dream of the night, and said to him, Behold, you are a dead man, because of the woman whom you have taken; for she is a man's wife.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yavo Elohim el-Avimelekh ba-chalom ha-lailah* — *and the Elohim came to Avimelekh in the dream of the night*. The verse is the **first occurrence in the Hebrew Bible of the night-dream-revelation formula** (see [divine-dream-communication-formula](#divine-dream-communication-formula)). The formula recurs as a structural type across the patriarchal and Joseph cycles (Gen 28:12 Jacob's ladder; Gen 31:24 Laban warned not to speak good-or-evil to Jacob; Gen 37:5-11 Joseph's dreams; Gen 40-41 Pharaoh's cupbearer, baker, and Pharaoh himself; cf. 1 Kgs 3:5 Solomon at Gibeon, the direct formula-parallel) and is one of the Hebrew Bible's principal modes of divine address to non-Israelite figures.

The parallel-structure with Num 12:6 (*im yihyeh nevi'akhem YHWH ba-mar'ah elav etvada ba-chalom adaber bo* — *if there is a prophet of YHWH among you, in a vision I make myself known to him, in a dream I speak with him*) makes explicit what this verse instances: the dream is the principal medium of prophetic-revelatory communication outside the Mosaic *peh-el-peh* face-to-face mode (Num 12:8). Husser 1999 *Dreams and Dream Narratives in the Biblical World* and Lichtenstein 1968 *JANES* 1 are the standard scholarly treatments; the ANE comparanda include the Mesopotamian *šuttu* dream-revelation literature and the Egyptian dream-books of the late New Kingdom (Papyrus Chester Beatty III).

The ASV's *in a dream of the night* (preserved here over modern smoothings *in a dream by night* / *in a night-time dream*) preserves the construct chain *chalom ha-lailah* visibly, treating the dream-of-the-night as a particular communicative medium rather than as a time-of-day adverbial.

paragraphs.text: וַאֲבִימֶ֕לֶךְ לֹ֥א קָרַ֖ב אֵלֶ֑יהָ וַיֹּאמַ֕ר אֲדֹנָ֕י הֲג֥וֹי גַּם־צַדִּ֖יק תַּהֲרֹֽג׃

i18n.en: Now Avimelekh had not come near her: and he said, Lord, will you slay even a righteous nation?

paragraphs.commentary: *Adonai ha-goy gam-tzaddiq taharog* — *Lord, will you slay even a righteous nation?* The verse is a deliberate verbal echo of Abraham's intercession at Gen 18:23-25 (*ha-af tispeh tzaddiq im-rasha; chalilah lekha la-asot ka-davar ha-ze* — *will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked; far be it from you to do such a thing*; see [abraham-intercession-bargaining](#abraham-intercession-bargaining)). The structural reversal is worth flagging: it is now the foreign king who takes up Abraham's stance against indiscriminate divine slaying — same *tzaddiq* lexeme, same indignant-vocative *Adonai*, same accusatory-interrogative form challenging divine justice. Avimelekh-the-non-Israelite-king is the chapter's moral voice; Abraham-the-patriarch will be the morally compromised figure (vv 9-10). Sarna (*JPS Genesis* 1989, p. 142) reads this as a deliberate compositional inversion of the previous chapter's intercession-scene.

paragraphs.text: הֲלֹ֨א ה֤וּא אָֽמַר־לִי֙ אֲחֹ֣תִי הִ֔וא וְהִֽיא־גַם־הִ֥וא אָֽמְרָ֖ה אָחִ֣י ה֑וּא בְּתָם־לְבָבִ֛י וּבְנִקְיֹ֥ן כַּפַּ֖י עָשִׂ֥יתִי זֹֽאת׃

i18n.en: Did he not himself say to me, She is my sister? and she, even she herself, said, He is my brother: in the integrity of my heart and in the cleanness of my hands I have done this.

paragraphs.commentary: *B-tom levavi u-v-niqyon kappai* — *in the integrity of my heart and in the cleanness of my hands*. The doubled-noun moral-innocence formula (see [b-tom-levav-u-v-niqyon-kappai-moral-innocence](#b-tom-levav-u-v-niqyon-kappai-moral-innocence)) is a fixed forensic-moral idiom. Cross-corpus parallels include Ps 24:4 *neqi kappayim u-var levav* (*clean of hands and pure of heart*), Ps 26:6 (washing of hands in innocence), Ps 73:13 (*ach riq zikiti levavi va-erchatz b-niqayon kappai*), and Job 22:30 (*niqyon kappekha*). The phrase recurs in shortened form (*tom levav* alone) at v 6 — Elohim's acknowledgment in the dream. ASV's *integrity / cleanness* register is preserved over modern smoothings (*blamelessness / innocence*) so that the doubled-construct legal form remains visible in English.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ אֵלָ֨יו הָֽאֱלֹהִ֜ים בַּחֲלֹ֗ם גַּ֣ם אָנֹכִ֤י יָדַ֙עְתִּי֙ כִּ֤י בְתָם־לְבָבְךָ֙ עָשִׂ֣יתָ זֹּ֔את וָאֶחְשֹׂ֧ךְ גַּם־אָנֹכִ֛י אֽוֹתְךָ֖ מֵחֲטוֹ־לִ֑י עַל־כֵּ֥ן לֹא־נְתַתִּ֖יךָ לִנְגֹּ֥עַ אֵלֶֽיהָ׃

i18n.en: And the Elohim said to him in the dream, Yes, I know that in the integrity of your heart you have done this, and I also withheld you from sinning against me: therefore I did not let you touch her.

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּ֗ה הָשֵׁ֤ב אֵֽשֶׁת־הָאִישׁ֙ כִּֽי־נָבִ֣יא ה֔וּא וְיִתְפַּלֵּ֥ל בַּֽעַדְךָ֖ וֶֽחְיֵ֑ה וְאִם־אֵֽינְךָ֣ מֵשִׁ֗יב דַּ֚ע כִּי־מ֣וֹת תָּמ֔וּת אַתָּ֖ה וְכָל־אֲשֶׁר־לָֽךְ׃

i18n.en: Now therefore restore the man's wife; for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for you, and you shall live: and if you do not restore her, know that you shall surely die, you, and all that are yours.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ki-navi hu v-yitpallel ba-adkha* — *for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for you*. The verse is one of the chapter's two foundational firsts: **the first occurrence of *navi* (prophet) in the Hebrew Bible** (see [navi-first-occurrence-abraham](#navi-first-occurrence-abraham)), paired with the first occurrence of *hithpallel* (to pray, intercede) at v 17 (see [hithpallel-first-prayer-occurrence](#hithpallel-first-prayer-occurrence)). The two firsts coincide structurally — the prophetic role is named (v 7) alongside the prophetic function the role discharges (v 17).

The lexical-and-historical significance is substantial. (a) The *navi* designation places Abraham in the prophetic stratum **before the Mosaic prophetic tradition begins** (Deut 18:15-18 will frame Moses as the prophetic model, but the title itself is older within the canonical sequence). (b) The function-definition delivered here is **intercessory**, not predictive: *v-yitpallel ba-adkha* — *and he shall pray on your behalf* — defines the prophet as the figure who stands between the deity and the threatened party and prays for the latter's deliverance. The prophetic-intercession model recurs at Exod 32:11-14 (Moses for Israel after the golden calf), Num 14:13-19 (Moses for Israel at Kadesh), 1 Sam 7:5 and 12:23 (Samuel for Israel), Jer 7:16 and 11:14 and 14:11 (the prophetic-intercession *prohibition* formula — YHWH telling Jeremiah *not* to pray for the people), and Amos 7:1-6 (the prophet talks YHWH down from two of the three threatened plagues). (c) The mouth uttering the title is the Elohim addressing a **foreign king** — the title is not first heard from within the Israelite tradition but spoken to an outsider.

The modern scholarly literature distinguishes the *navi* (the one who is called, or the one who calls — both etymologies are defended) from the older *ro'eh* (seer, 1 Sam 9:9) and *chozeh* (visionary). Lindblom 1962 *Prophecy in Ancient Israel*, Wilson 1980 *Prophecy and Society in Ancient Israel*, Petersen 2002 *The Prophetic Literature*, and Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 all treat the Abraham-as-first-*navi* designation as canonically deliberate. Speiser (*Anchor Bible Genesis*, 1964) renders *navi* here as *spokesman* — preserving the called-and-sent etymology — but the ASV-baseline *prophet* is preserved here as the standard scholarly rendering; the function-definition is carried by the verse's own paratactic structure (*navi hu v-yitpallel* — *he is a prophet, and he shall pray*) rather than by the title's translation.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם אֲבִימֶ֜לֶךְ בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּקְרָא֙ לְכָל־עֲבָדָ֔יו וַיְדַבֵּ֛ר אֶת־כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֥ים הָאֵ֖לֶּה בְּאָזְנֵיהֶ֑ם וַיִּֽירְא֥וּ הָאֲנָשִׁ֖ים מְאֹֽד׃

i18n.en: And Avimelekh rose early in the morning, and called all his servants, and spoke all these things in their ears: and the men were greatly afraid.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֨א אֲבִימֶ֜לֶךְ לְאַבְרָהָ֗ם וַיֹּ֨אמֶר ל֜וֹ מֶֽה־עָשִׂ֤יתָ לָּ֙נוּ֙ וּמֶֽה־חָטָ֣אתִי לָ֔ךְ כִּֽי־הֵבֵ֧אתָ עָלַ֛י וְעַל־מַמְלַכְתִּ֖י חֲטָאָ֣ה גְדֹלָ֑ה מַעֲשִׂים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא־יֵֽעָשׂ֔וּ עָשִׂ֖יתָ עִמָּדִֽי׃

i18n.en: Then Avimelekh called Abraham, and said to him, What have you done to us? and wherein have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin? You have done deeds to me that ought not to be done.

paragraphs.commentary: The king's rebuke echoes Pharaoh's rebuke at Gen 12:18 (*mah-zot asita li* — *what is this you have done to me*) and prefigures Abimelekh's later rebuke of Isaac at Gen 26:10 — the type-scene's recurring rebuke-of-the-patriarch element. The cumulative effect across the three episodes is to mark the patriarchs as morally compromised in their dealings with the foreign kings, and to give the foreign kings the moral voice in each scene.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר אֲבִימֶ֖לֶךְ אֶל־אַבְרָהָ֑ם מָ֣ה רָאִ֔יתָ כִּ֥י עָשִׂ֖יתָ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּֽה׃

i18n.en: And Avimelekh said to Abraham, What did you see, that you have done this thing?

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ אַבְרָהָ֔ם כִּ֣י אָמַ֗רְתִּי רַ֚ק אֵין־יִרְאַ֣ת אֱלֹהִ֔ים בַּמָּק֖וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה וַהֲרָג֖וּנִי עַל־דְּבַ֥ר אִשְׁתִּֽי׃

i18n.en: And Abraham said, Because I thought, Surely the fear of the Elohim is not in this place; and they will slay me for my wife's sake.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Raq ein yir'at Elohim ba-maqom ha-ze* — *surely the fear of the Elohim is not in this place*. The *yir'at Elohim* / *yir'at YHWH* motif is the Hebrew Bible's principal designation of moral restraint, prudent reverence, and covenantal-ethical conscience (see [yirat-elohim-moral-restraint-motif](#yirat-elohim-moral-restraint-motif)). The cross-corpus chain is long and load-bearing: Gen 22:12 *ata yadati ki yere Elohim ata* — the Aqedah's closing word, *now I know that you fear the Elohim*; Gen 42:18 — Joseph to his brothers, *et-ha-Elohim ani yare*; Exod 1:17, 1:21 — the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, whose fear-of-the-Elohim disobedience to Pharaoh saves Israelite infants; Exod 20:20 — at Sinai, *in order that the fear of him may be before you*; Job 1:1, 1:8, 2:3 — Job characterized as *yere Elohim*; and across Proverbs the wisdom-tradition axiom *yir'at YHWH reshit da'at* (Prov 1:7, 9:10).

**The chapter's irony is sharp.** Abraham assumed there was no fear-of-the-Elohim in Gerar, and acted to protect himself accordingly; the chapter has just demonstrated that in fact Avimelekh fears the Elohim (he refrains from touching Sarah on hearing the dream, vv 6-8) and the deception was unnecessary — and indeed harmful (it endangered Avimelekh and his household, v 18). The narrative's evaluation of Abraham's prudential calculation is implicit but pointed. Becker 1965 *Gottesfurcht im Alten Testament* is the standard treatment of the motif; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 reads this verse as the chapter's central irony.

paragraphs.text: וְגַם־אָמְנָ֗ה אֲחֹתִ֤י בַת־אָבִי֙ הִ֔וא אַ֖ךְ לֹ֣א בַת־אִמִּ֑י וַתְּהִי־לִ֖י לְאִשָּֽׁה׃

i18n.en: And moreover she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife.

paragraphs.commentary:
*V-gam omnah achoti bat-avi hi, akh lo bat-imi* — *and moreover she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother*. The verse is the **only place in the patriarchal narrative where the half-sister claim of the wife-sister deception is explicitly defended**, and it is offered defensively under questioning. The claim makes Abraham's earlier statement at Gen 12:13 (*imri-na achoti at*) **technically true** — Sarah is, on this account, his half-sister; see the discussion at [imri-na-achoti-at](#imri-na-achoti-at).

The modern critical-scholarship reading treats v 12 with caution: the half-sister datum appears only here, only after rebuke, and only in the chapter most plausibly assigned to the E source on the classical documentary hypothesis. Speiser 1964, Westermann 1985, Sarna 1989, and Hamilton 1990 all flag the verse as potentially apologetic redaction — material introduced precisely to mitigate the deception. The Mosaic-law prohibition of half-sister marriage (Lev 18:9, 20:17, Deut 27:22) post-dates the patriarchal period within the canonical sequence, so Abraham's claim does not on its face violate any law the narrative recognizes as binding on him; the harmonization works at the level of legal chronology. The rabbinic tradition (Gen Rab 41:2; Rashi) takes the verse at face value as authentic Abrahamic genealogy and treats Abraham's earlier deception as a *partial truth under duress*. The two readings are not mutually exclusive — both are documented in the [imri-na-achoti-at](#imri-na-achoti-at) entry.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֞י כַּאֲשֶׁ֧ר הִתְע֣וּ אֹתִ֗י אֱלֹהִים֮ מִבֵּ֣ית אָבִי֒ וָאֹמַ֣ר לָ֔הּ זֶ֣ה חַסְדֵּ֔ךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר תַּעֲשִׂ֖י עִמָּדִ֑י אֶ֤ל כָּל־הַמָּקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָב֣וֹא שָׁ֔מָּה אִמְרִי־לִ֖י אָחִ֥י הֽוּא׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when the Elohim caused me to wander from my father's house, that I said to her, This is your kindness which you shall show to me: at every place where we shall come, say of me, He is my brother.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Hit'u oti Elohim mi-beit avi* — *the Elohim caused me to wander from my father's house*. The verb *hit'u* (hiphil 3mp of *t-ʿ-h*, *to err / wander*) is **morphologically plural** — *they caused me to wander* — with Elohim as a plural-syntactic-agreement subject. The chapter contains one of the Hebrew Bible's clearest cases where Elohim takes a plural verb (other widely-cited cases: Gen 35:7 *niglu elav ha-Elohim*; Exod 32:4, 8 *eleh elohekha Yisrael asher he'elukha me-eretz Mitzrayim*; 2 Sam 7:23 / 1 Chron 17:21 *halkhu Elohim lifdot lo l-am*). The verse is editorially significant for the broader project policy on Elohim-with-plural-verbs, but the WoH translation here follows the ASV-baseline singular smoothing (*the Elohim caused me*) for English readability, and surfaces the morphological-plural datum in commentary rather than in the translation text.

The modern critical scholarship treats most such cases as singular-meaning despite plural form: NJPS, Speiser 1964, and the standard reference grammars (GKC §145i; Joüon-Muraoka §150f) read them as *plural of majesty* or as *grammatical plural with semantic singular*. The dissenting position — that the plural verb-agreement preserves an older polytheistic stratum — is associated with the History-of-Religions School (Gunkel; Wellhausen) and with the modern divine-council scholarship (Mullen 1980 *The Divine Council*; Smith 2001 *The Origins of Biblical Monotheism*). The WoH glossary's [elohim-as-translation](#elohim-as-translation) entry's article-convention does not preempt either reading; the chapter editor's note is to flag this verse for future Reviewer attention on whether a project-policy decision on plural-verb cases should be settled by a dedicated glossary entry.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח אֲבִימֶ֜לֶךְ צֹ֣אן וּבָקָ֗ר וַעֲבָדִים֙ וּשְׁפָחֹ֔ת וַיִּתֵּ֖ן לְאַבְרָהָ֑ם וַיָּ֣שֶׁב ל֔וֹ אֵ֖ת שָׂרָ֥ה אִשְׁתּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Avimelekh took sheep and oxen, and menservants and maidservants, and gave them to Abraham, and restored him Sarah his wife.

paragraphs.commentary: The gift-and-restoration formula parallels Pharaoh's at Gen 12:16, 19-20 — same inventory items (sheep, oxen, servants, maidservants), same restoration of the wife. The type-scene's recurring gift-and-restoration element is the king's restitution after the deception is uncovered; Avimelekh adds (at v 15) the offer of the land itself, which Pharaoh did not.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲבִימֶ֔לֶךְ הִנֵּ֥ה אַרְצִ֖י לְפָנֶ֑יךָ בַּטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֶ֖יךָ שֵֽׁב׃

i18n.en: And Avimelekh said, Behold, my land is before you: dwell where it pleases you.

paragraphs.text: וּלְשָׂרָ֣ה אָמַ֗ר הִנֵּ֨ה נָתַ֜תִּי אֶ֤לֶף כֶּ֙סֶף֙ לְאָחִ֔יךְ הִנֵּ֤ה הוּא־לָךְ֙ כְּס֣וּת עֵינַ֔יִם לְכֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתָּ֑ךְ וְאֵ֥ת כֹּ֖ל וְנֹכָֽחַת׃

i18n.en: And to Sarah he said, Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother: behold, it is for you a covering of the eyes to all that are with you; and in respect of all you are righted.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Hineh hu lakh kesut eynayim* — *behold, it is for you a covering of the eyes*. The phrase *kesut eynayim* is a **hapax** in the Hebrew Bible (see [kesut-eynayim-vindication-formula](#kesut-eynayim-vindication-formula)) and its idiomatic sense is genuinely contested. Three principal modern readings: (a) **vindication / public exoneration** — the thousand pieces of silver function as a public sign that no one looking on can impute disgrace to Sarah; this is the dominant modern reading (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989, Speiser *Anchor Bible Genesis* 1964; cf. ASV *a covering of the eyes*); (b) **veil / face-covering** — a literal cloth purchased with the silver, as a marker of restored honorable-married-woman status (Rashi; some medieval commentators); (c) **bribe / hush-money** — a minority critical reading where the silver buys the silence of onlookers (some early 20th-c. critical commentators).

The closing phrase *ve-et kol ve-nokhachat* (*and in respect of all you are righted*) is also obscure — the verb *yakach* (niphal participle *nokhachat*) carries the sense of being-put-right / vindicated / judged-correct, but the syntax is difficult (Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 reads the text as possibly corrupt; NJPS hedges *and you are cleared before everyone*). The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline literal *a covering of the eyes ... in respect of all you are righted*, with the three-reading dispute carried in the apparatus.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֥ל אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים וַיִּרְפָּ֨א אֱלֹהִ֜ים אֶת־אֲבִימֶ֧לֶךְ וְאֶת־אִשְׁתּ֛וֹ וְאַמְהֹתָ֖יו וַיֵּלֵֽדוּ׃

i18n.en: And Abraham prayed to the Elohim; and the Elohim healed Avimelekh, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bore children.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Va-yitpallel Avraham el ha-Elohim* — *and Abraham prayed to the Elohim*. The verse delivers the second of the chapter's two foundational firsts: **the first occurrence in the Hebrew Bible of *hithpallel* (the hithpael of *p-l-l*, *to pray, to intercede*)** — paired with the first occurrence of *navi* at v 7 (see [hithpallel-first-prayer-occurrence](#hithpallel-first-prayer-occurrence) and [navi-first-occurrence-abraham](#navi-first-occurrence-abraham)). The two firsts coincide structurally: the prophet promised in v 7 now performs the prophetic act that v 7 defined. The chapter is the canonical Hebrew Bible *function-definition* of the prophet as intercessor.

The lexeme *hithpallel* (reflexive-iterative-hithpael of *p-l-l*) becomes the Hebrew Bible's principal verb for petitionary and intercessory prayer. The cross-corpus distribution is forward-loaded: Num 11:2, 21:7 (Moses for the people); 1 Sam 1:10, 1:12, 2:1 (Hannah); 1 Sam 7:5, 8:6, 12:19, 12:23 (Samuel, including the load-bearing *chalilah li me-chato la-YHWH me-chadol l-hitpallel ba-adkhem* — *far be it from me to sin against YHWH by ceasing to pray for you*); 1 Kgs 8:28-54 (Solomon's temple-dedication prayer, the longest *hithpallel* sequence in the corpus); 2 Kgs 19:15, 20:2, Isa 37:15, 38:2 (Hezekiah); Jer 7:16, 11:14, 14:11 (the prophetic-intercession-*prohibition* formula); Dan 9:4, 9:20; Neh 1:4, 1:6, 2:4. Greenberg 1983 *Biblical Prose Prayer* is the standard treatment; Miller 1994 *They Cried to the Lord* and Balentine 1993 *Prayer in the Hebrew Bible* extend the analysis. The etymology of *hithpallel* is debated — HALOT glosses *to intercede*; Greenberg argues for *to assess oneself* (taking the reflexive seriously); the broader West-Semitic root *p-l-l* (judge, intervene, mediate) underwrites both readings. The translation preserves the ASV-baseline *prayed* over the more lexically-precise *interceded* on the grounds that the standard rendering captures the function (and the function-definition is carried by the v 7 framing); the nuance is recorded in the entry.

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־עָצֹ֤ר עָצַר֙ יְהוָ֔ה בְּעַ֥ד כָּל־רֶ֖חֶם לְבֵ֣ית אֲבִימֶ֑לֶךְ עַל־דְּבַ֥ר שָׂרָ֖ה אֵ֥שֶׁת אַבְרָהָֽם׃

i18n.en: For YHWH had fast closed up every womb of the house of Avimelekh, because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ki-atzor atzar YHWH be-ad kol-rechem le-veit Avimelekh* — *for YHWH had fast closed up every womb of the house of Avimelekh*. The doubled construction *atzor atzar* (infinitive absolute + finite verb of *atzar* — *restrain, hold back, close up*) is the Hebrew Bible's standard intensification pattern for emphatic verb-action; ASV's *fast closed up* preserves the doubling visibly. The chapter's structural movement — patriarch endangered → foreign king afflicted with closed wombs → patriarch intercedes (v 17) → wombs reopen — is reconstructed retrospectively at this closing verse, which functions as the chapter's etiological coda.

The *closed-wombs-as-divine-sanction* motif (see [atzar-rechem-closed-wombs-divine-sanction](#atzar-rechem-closed-wombs-divine-sanction)) recurs across the matriarchal-barrenness pattern of the patriarchal and pre-monarchic corpus: Gen 11:30 (Sarai herself — the unresolved barrenness that hangs over the entire Abraham cycle and resolves only at Gen 21); Gen 25:21 (Rebekah, whose barrenness Isaac entreats YHWH for); Gen 29:31 (the Leah / Rachel inversion — *va-yare YHWH ki s'nu'ah Leah va-yiftach et-rachmah v-Rachel aqarah* — Leah's womb opened, Rachel's closed); Judg 13:2-3 (Manoah's wife, the mother of Samson); 1 Sam 1:5-6 (*va-YHWH sagar rachmah* — Hannah, with the same *sagar*-the-womb verbal collocation). Brichto 1973 *HUCA* 44 on the womb-theology of the matriarchal cycle is the standard treatment; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* and Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* extend the analysis. The chapter's irony recurs at the structural level: the wife-sister deception undertaken to protect the patriarchal couple has produced precisely the barrenness-on-the-foreign-household that the cycle ordinarily reserves for the matriarchs themselves.
